title: A Borel Lie algebra selects one of each opposite pair of torus roots
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $F$, and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Write $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga] for commutative $F$-algebras $A$. Lie algebras are tangent spaces at the identity, with the adjoint action obtained by differentiating conjugation. A smooth group is unipotent if its geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. A reductive group is smooth and connected with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$; it is maximal if it is contained in no larger torus subgroup. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial, and a Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. Let $G$ be reductive, $T\subseteq G$ a maximal torus and $B\subseteq G$ a Borel subgroup containing $T$. Let $\Phi$ be the nontrivial characters $\alpha:T\to\mathbf G_m$ occurring in $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, and let $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ be their weight spaces. Then $\Phi$ is finite, $-\alpha\in\Phi$ for each $\alpha\in\Phi$, and, setting $\Psi_B=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)\}$, one has
$$\operatorname{Lie}(B)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Psi_B}\mathfrak g_\alpha,\qquad \#(\Psi_B\cap\{\alpha,-\alpha\})=1\quad(\alpha\in\Phi).$$
The weights are characters of the torus, not differentials of characters; no restriction on the characteristic of $F$ is imposed.

source.place: Lemma 21.28, printed p.433; Theorem 21.11(b),(c), printed pp.428--429, and its use in the proof of Proposition 21.29, printed p.434.

proof.text: Apply the reductive rank-one theorem to $(G,T)$. It gives a finite decomposition $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$, one-dimensional root spaces, and $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ for every root $\alpha$. In particular $\Phi$ is finite and stable under negation. Fix a root $\alpha$ for the next three steps; when there are no roots these steps are vacuous.

Let $S=T_\alpha$ be the largest subtorus of $\ker\alpha$ and $H=C_G(S)$. The rank-one theorem makes $H$ reductive of semisimple rank one with maximal torus $T$. Apply the centralizer-intersection theorem with $S\subseteq T\subseteq B$: the scheme intersection $D=B\times_GH$ is a smooth connected solvable Borel subgroup of $H$, and it contains $T$. All of these are scheme-theoretic inclusions.

source.place: Lemma 21.28, p.433, invoking Theorem 17.46, pp.365--366 (restated in 17.72).

proof.text: Use the rank-one pair classification to identify $(H,T)$ with $(\mathbf G_m^r\times M,\mathbf G_m^r\times D_M)$, where $M$ is $\operatorname{SL}_2$, $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ or $\operatorname{GL}_2$ and $D_M$ is its standard diagonal torus. Act on the projective line of lines in $F^2$ by the matrix factor, with the central torus acting trivially; scalar matrices act trivially, so the action descends in the PGL case. This is the usual algebraic projective action. The projective line is nonempty, finite type (its two affine-line charts), and proper by the cited projective-space theorem. Apply the solvable fixed-point theorem to $D$ acting on this line: some line $L$ is fixed scheme-theoretically. Since $T\subseteq D$, $L$ is diagonal-torus invariant. The only such lines are $Fe_1$ and $Fe_2$: for a vector with both coordinates nonzero, a diagonal element with unequal coordinate ratio moves the line. In the SL case choose $s$ with $s^2\ne1$; such an $s$ exists even in characteristic two because $F$ is algebraically closed. Thus $D$ is contained, as a group scheme, in an upper or lower triangular stabilizer $Q$ of $H$. Each $Q$ is smooth connected solvable: its variety is a product of a split torus and $\mathbf A^1$, and the diagonal homomorphism has commutative torus image and kernel $\mathbf G_a$. Maximality of the Borel $D$ in $H$ gives $D=Q$.

source.place: Lemma 21.28, p.433; rank-one description in 20.20, pp.414--415. Explicit line-stabilizer argument as in Example 17.7 and Theorem 17.9, p.354, using Corollary 17.3, p.353.

proof.text: Compute tangent spaces in these matrix models. The two off-diagonal tangent directions have torus characters $\pm2\chi$ for SL2, $\pm\chi$ for PGL2 (diagonal ratio $\chi$), and $\pm(e_1-e_2)$ for GL2. For PGL2 its tangent space is $\mathfrak{gl}_2/FI$; the off-diagonal classes survive in every characteristic. An upper triangular $Q$ contains just the upper direction and a lower triangular $Q$ just the lower direction. To identify these directions inside $\mathfrak g$, write $\alpha=ma$ with $a$ primitive in the free character lattice of $T$, using character antiduality. Extend $a$ to an integral basis; then $S$ is given by first torus coordinate $1$, and a character is trivial on $S$ exactly when it is an integral multiple of $a$. A tangent vector belongs to $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ precisely when its dual-number point centralizes $S$ after every algebra extension, equivalently when it is $S$-fixed. Hence $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$, by the rational-multiple assertion of step 1. Thus the two off-diagonal directions are exactly $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ and $\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$, possibly with labels exchanged. Tangents commute with this fibre product: a dual-number point in $D=B\times_GH$ is precisely one in both $B$ and $H$. Consequently exactly one of $\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ is contained in $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(b), pp.428--430; standard matrix models in 21.4--21.6, pp.425--426; character antiduality in 12.9 and 12.23; dual-number description of fixed tangents in 10.34.

proof.text: Finally $\mathfrak b=\operatorname{Lie}(B)$ is a $T$-stable subspace containing $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. For $v\in\mathfrak b$, write its weight decomposition $v=v_0+\sum v_\beta$ from step 1. Its coaction is $v_0\otimes1+\sum v_\beta\otimes e_\beta$ in $\mathfrak b\otimes F[X^*(T)]$. Comparing the independent Laurent monomials $1,e_\beta$ shows that each $v_\beta$ lies in $\mathfrak b$. Each intersection $\mathfrak b\cap\mathfrak g_\beta$ is zero or the whole space because the latter is one-dimensional. Therefore $\mathfrak b=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Psi_B}\mathfrak g_\beta$. Step 4 gives exactly one element of $\Psi_B$ in every opposite pair. These are distinct characters: $\alpha=-\alpha$ would give $2\alpha=0$ in a free integer lattice, contradicting $\alpha\ne0$. This proves the cardinality assertion, including in characteristic two. If $\Phi$ is empty, the same subspace argument gives $\mathfrak b=\operatorname{Lie}(T)$.

source.place: Theorem 12.12, pp.234--235 (coaction coefficients); Lemma 21.28 and proof of Proposition 21.29, pp.433--434.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 21.28 and Theorem 21.11(b), pp.428--433; the rank-one step is expanded using the fixed-point argument of 17.7--17.9 and the explicit matrix classification.
